comments.author: @Gargamel-n-Rudmilla
comments.text:
I think the methodology of reinforcement learning is to a fist order approximation the right approach because we see this in nature, and this is through the tree of life.
For human level or animal level ( that live in groups) intelligence, several other methods should be added to complement the reward strategy.  
These are the ability to assess risk (upside and downside ) and also cost and benefit. 
These four capabilities must be assessed in the short/now time frame, medium term, and long term since for living organisms, time has value for obvious reasons.
For synthetic entities such as AI, do they even understand what time and physics are, given these things have a completely different effect on them and do they understand how it affect humans and other organic life. 
They may not need to in some applications, but time must be instilled in them to have a value. 
If the output of their work takes a relatively longer time, then it's value to others who have asked it to complete a task must be greater. Or the task would have been done better by a human or in a shorter time or cost less.
Obviously, if it could not be done by a human in the first place, then time is not really an issue or cost, just the accuracy of the result.

comments.author: @stcredzero
comments.text: So, if anyone is familiar with computers optimizing in ways humans wouldn't ever think of, this goes all the way back to Eurisko in 1980's and the Trillion Credit Squadron Traveller RPG wargame tournament. We see such novel solutions in the recent AI enhanced theorem solvers and AIs tackling math competition problems. We see this in the novel tactics created by board game AIs. What we don't want, is to see such a "novel solution" appear as an implemented action in an AI agent that controls considerable resources. As the optimization capability of AI agents increase, and the resources they control increase, the probability that some AI will see and implement a "novel solution" we really, really wouldn't like also increases.
